item.title: Is Psychology Measuring Introversion All Wrong?
item.description:
Introversion

Is Psychology Measuring Introversion All Wrong?

New research suggests introversion is more than simply low extraversion.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • The Big Five defines introversion as low extraversion, potentially missing its distinct qualities.
  • A 2025 study found Big Five introversion did not predict positive motivations for solitude.
  • STAR separates introversion into social, thinking, anxious, and restrained dimensions.
Source: Nicola Barts/Pexels

It used to be that if you wanted to know if someone was an introvert, you handed them a personality questionnaire, and oh, by the way, it was definitely built on the Big Five model, the dominant framework in personality science since the 1980s. Their score on the extraversion scale would have told you what you wanted to know.

But newer research is challenging the Big Five’s position as the best measure of introversion. If the critique holds, it could mean that decades of findings about introverts may have been skewed in ways I’ll explain.

The Problem With “Low Extraversion”

The biggest problem is that the Big Five doesn’t actually measure introversion directly, which very well may mean, in effect, that it is not measuring introversion at all. You see, what the Big Five does is measure extraversion and then, believe it or not, treats introversion as the absence of extraversion. So introversion, within this model, is the low end of the extraversion dial. But that kind of makes sense, right?

Yet it paints a certain picture. A person with low extraversion is (look closely at the words I’m about to use) reserved, inhibited, quiet, or withdrawn. In the words of researchers Valerie Thomas and Pauline Nelson, the Big Five assigns “solely negative characteristics” to introverts. Oh great. Thanks. In other words, it defines introverts by what they lack rather than by the qualities and functional characteristics that they actually possess.

That’s like defining calm as “low anger,” by the way. Which would miss something essential about the experience of being calm, wouldn’t it?

Enter the STAR Introversion Scale

So, in 2014, psychologist Jonathan Cheek and colleagues proposed the STAR Introversion Scale, measuring four distinct flavors of introversion (Cool, Jon et al., 2014):

  • Social introversion, which is, in their definition, someone with a genuine preference for solitude or small groups (not a fear of social situations).
  • Thinking introversion, which means someone with a rich inner life, including introspection, imagination, and comfort hanging out inside their own mind for a while.
  • Anxious introversion, which includes shyness, self-consciousness, and rumination in social settings (wait, what?).
  • Restrained introversion refers to someone with a deliberate, measured approach, like thinking before speaking, observing before jumping in, that sort of thing.

The Big Five Model vs. the STAR Model

In a 2025 study published in the Journal of Personality, Thomas and Nelson put these two approaches head-to-head, examining which better predicted solitude-seeking behavior, arguably the most signature introverted tendency (I also so argue).

Big Five introversion showed no relationship at all with positive motivation for solitude. None. Zero. Zilch. It didn’t predict wanting to be alone, and worse, under the Big Five, it was low introversion (meaning higher extraversion) that predicted actually spending more time alone. Crazy, eh? This study found that, by the Big Five’s very own logic, extraverts are the ones who are out there in the world seeking solitude for themselves, so something had clearly gone sideways.

The STAR model, on the other hand, told a coherent story about solitude. “Social introversion” predicted both the desire for and the amount of time spent alone, while curiously but understandably, “thinking introversion,” and only thinking introversion, was associated with genuinely wanting solitude, and “anxious introversion” predicted wanting solitude for negative avoidance reasons, which all makes sense to me.

When the study incorporated STAR and Big Five data and analyzed various fancy comparisons statistically, the conclusions that resulted began to indicate that perhaps where the Big Five had claimed introversion, it had actually all along been capturing something much closer to what would be better described as neuroticism. (Whoa.)

Source: Siarhei Nester/Pexels

Why This Matters Beyond Academia

I can answer that! Well, you see, if clinical screening tools rely on Big Five-based formulations of introversion, a therapist might interpret a patient’s solitude-seeking as a symptom of a disorder rather than merely their preference. They might cast a thinking introvert who recharges alone as socially withdrawn. Alternatively, they might underestimate the functional impact of an anxious introvert’s distress given that it’s literally part of a normalized trait score, when in fact, it is an indication of clinically concerning functioning and treatable patterns. Ah, you see now?

In workplaces, the Big Five framework feeds a narrative in which introversion is a deficit to be managed, such as the stereotypical quiet employee who needs to “come out of their shell.” In reality, there is not necessarily a defensive shell at all but, rather, likely a vital interior life. Such confusion risks a perpetuation in varying forms and degrees of, in effect, pathologizing perfectly functional ways of being human.

What the STAR Model Gets Right (and Might Get Wrong)

To me, the STAR’s great contribution is carving out space for thinking introversion, a dimension completely invisible to the Big Five, for introverts who don’t avoid people out of anxiety but do also gravitate toward ideas, reflection, imagination, and, thus, toward solitude. This is arguably at the heart of what most self-identified introverts mean when they say “introvert” to describe themselves (can I get an amen?).

Source: PSRVSKY PI/Pexels

But still, clearly the STAR model has its own vulnerabilities. It is relatively new, developed by a small research group, and has had as-yet-limited independent validation across diverse populations (equity!). And “anxious introversion” is easily debatable. If it so strongly correlates with neuroticism, is it even an aspect of introversion, or is it really something altogether different, albeit related, that should be measured separately?

A Field in Transition

Whatever the case on the nuances, it is clear enough that the STAR is bringing a serious challenge to whether the Big Five, for all its strengths, has introversion right.

As I’ve alluded, emerging evidence suggests it does not—that it has been measuring only a shadow of introversion, defined by deficit and tinged with pathology, while missing the fuller, more textured reality, so I am appreciative of new perspectives.

This new conversation is just beginning, but for the many millions (including myself, hi) who have long felt that their introversion is something richer than “not extraverted enough,” the science may thankfully, finally, hopefully, be catching up.

item.title: What Young Adults Want Parents to Know About Them
item.description:
Parenting

What Young Adults Want Parents to Know About Them

Understanding themes of struggle among young adults.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • I learn a lot from my young adult patients.
  • Some of them have difficulty in communicating genuinely with their parents.
  • Here are some of the messages that your young adult may wish they could share with you.
Woman Model
Source: Image by JerzyGórecki from Pixabay

I am a psychologist who helps to run an Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) for young adults ages 18-26. These young people are facing mental health challenges that temporarily prevent them from enjoying their lives and relationships to the fullest extent they might. They also may be struggling with independence, as well as career or college progression. Here are some of the themes that I have heard consistently over the past few years. I hope it helps you to connect with and support your young adult children.

I do care about my future. If I am taking a leave of absence from college or am struggling with keeping or finding a job, it is not because I do not care. I care very much, actually. However, I am struggling with anxiety, depression, or other mental health concerns that need to be addressed before I can resume my journey.

I may not always like you, but I do love you. We have spent a lot of time together over the years, and it has not always been easy. In fact, we may disagree about a lot of things. However, that does not mean that I do not love you. Yes, I can not like you at times and still love you. Please remember that.

I want you to listen and see me for who I am. My personality and values are very important to me. I may not have everything figured out yet, and I am still learning about myself and the world, but I ask that you respect me for who I am today. Ask questions and be curious about what is important to me. If you ask in an open, loving way, I am happy to let you into my world.

I am frightened of the future, so please do not minimize the state of the world I am inheriting. Let’s be honest, the older generations have not left us with a world that is thriving and well. Selfish politicians, wars, climate change — all of this is stressful to me. So, yes, I have lost faith in “the system.” And can you blame me? Please be sympathetic when I am discouraged about the state of the world.

The world is different now than it was when you were my age (and not in a good way). It is a difficult time to be a young adult. With the introduction of AI and the comparisons on social media, life is particularly stressful for me. Yes, you had your own stressors, but please know that what we are dealing with now is new territory. No one knows where it will lead, which is stressful and scary for me.

Online friends are real friends too. I know you may not understand because the world is different today, but connecting with others online can be meaningful too. Especially while living through the pandemic, we had to get creative in how we meet and interact with others. Sometimes online connection feels safer and easier, actually.

Please, never give up on me. I know I am going through a difficult time. I may be struggling with my next steps academically, professionally, or personally. That does not mean that I have failed or that I will struggle my whole life. I just need some help and support now. I am excited for what is next but may need to heal and regroup first. Please stay in my corner as I prepare for what’s next.

item.title: Why Reconciliation Fails (and What Actually Makes It Work)
item.description:
Relationships

Why Reconciliation Fails (and What Actually Makes It Work)

Am I trying to get the old relationship back, or willing to build a new one?

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • Most reconciliations fail when one person can't hear how the other sees them without defending themselves.
  • The healing that makes reconciliation possible is the same healing that lets you be OK if it never arrives.
  • Real reconciliation isn't about restoring the past. It's about building something new that both can live in.

It seems family estrangement is showing up everywhere lately on social media. In particular, we see numerous headlines of adult children going “no contact." And, to some extent, the statistics support this observation.

A 2024 Harris Poll showed about half of American adults are estranged from at least one close relative, with 35 percent estranged from an immediate family member, such as a parent or sibling. Cornell sociologist Karl Pillemer estimates that 67 million Americans are estranged and that more than 4 in 10 will experience it at some point in their lives.

With this growing reality, reconnection often becomes a focus for one or both parties after estrangement, raising two very important questions. Firstly, why does family reconciliation so often break down, and secondly, what helps reconciliation succeed?

Are Words the Problem?

If you're estranged and searching for a way to reconnect, you may be feeling and carrying around a particular type of hope. Despite previous unsuccessful attempts to close the gap, you picture it going differently this time. You work to convince yourself that if you could only find the right words, everything would be fixed. But it isn’t.

After more than a decade of working in this field, I've discovered that words might not matter as much as we think they do. What actually determines how these conversations go is whether two people can stay emotionally present when words start to hurt, and to stay open, as opposed to shutting down or exchanging salvos, when things get tough.

What I see is that when one person describes your behavior in a way that’s painful to hear, you feel discomfort. In many cases, your body reacts instantly, before your mind has a chance to process the words. The other person hasn’t even finished their sentence, and you're already overwhelmed with the urge to respond, in all likelihood, with a counterattack. And most of the time, it doesn't feel like defensiveness from the inside. It probably feels like protecting yourself.

However, for the person who has worked up the courage to say the hard, painful thing, the message becomes that being honest isn't safe. And, therefore, the relationship isn't safe. And, until it is, repair cannot happen.

This is where I see many reconciliation attempts falter and stall. The fact that it’s even attempted underscores something incredibly important. Someone cares enough to give it a try. The unfortunate reality is that the well-intentioned bid for reconnection fails because of an inability to hear the other’s experience without the need to defend, deny, or deflect. This is at the heart of the problem. Only when it’s recognized and addressed can a space for genuine reconnection be created.

What Part Belongs to You?

Let me give you an example. A woman had chosen estrangement from her mother. Over time, her mother would reach out periodically. Each time, conversations started like an apology but quickly disintegrated into explanations that felt like justifications. Recollections only accommodated one set of experiences, the mother’s. Following each conversation, the daughter felt like nothing had changed. Each failed attempt increased the gap even further.

In order to make sense of this recurring pattern, the daughter turned to therapy and, through that process, became aware that she’d allowed her own healing to become dependent on a mother who might never want to or be able to hear her in the way she needed.

She longed for her mother to listen, acknowledge her childhood experiences, and take responsibility. But, repeatedly, that craved-for moment remained painfully elusive. So, she decided to stop waiting for something external that might never come and started healing anyway.

When the next reconnection attempt eventually happened, there was little to no expectation. Once she let go of needing her mother to own the past, things changed. She still received the same excuses, and the defensiveness remained, but now the daughter viewed both in a different light. She saw armor that had always been there. Armor that, importantly, she came to realise, had nothing to do with her.

In reality, the relationship remained far from what the daughter really longed for. For years, she’d hoped her mother would turn up to the conversation without armor and had weighted her expectations accordingly. Ultimately, it had become clear to her that her mother might never be capable of staying emotionally present and open. The only way to break the deadlock was to be a different daughter.

In making that decision, she and her mother embarked on a new relationship, one where she had created her own conditions for safety. One where she was emotionally present and open, and where, little by little, repair became possible.

Strangely, this isn't unusual. Research from the Family Estrangement & Reconciliation Project found this pattern spanning hundreds of successful reconciliations. Often, the people who rebuilt their relationships weren't the ones who finally got the listening, recognition, and understanding they'd been waiting for. They were the ones who embraced the importance of letting go of never-to-be-met expectations from an irreconcilable shared past.

So, on one hand, reconciliation could be seen as an attempt to reclaim and redirect the past. On the other hand, it can also become the foundation for something new and different. And, with the latter of these two possibilities, it doesn’t mean saying everything that happened in the past was fine. Nor does it mean that one’s experiences are unimportant. It simply means that one can finally put down things that should never been carried in the first place, so that healing and growth can happen.

Where Real Reconciliation Begins

I don't talk about this from theory alone. I have been estranged from a parent myself. I know how long the road back to rebuilding a stable relationship can be.

It might seem counterintuitive, but wherever you are in your journey, travel as lightly as possible. Carry fewer expectations, explanations, and justifications. Before ever considering the words you might use to try and bridge the gap between you and an estranged loved one, take a look at what you’re bringing with you.

To what extent the other person meets you halfway is largely beyond your control. That said, turning up to the conversation armed with a deeper degree of self-awareness, emotional grounding, and a commitment to healing that isn’t conditional on what the other person does or doesn’t do can often bring reconciliation within reach.

item.title: What Is "Emotional Regulation" for Parents?
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

What Is "Emotional Regulation" for Parents?

And what are steps to finding your emotional balance as a parent?

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • Parents need education and skills to regulate their emotions, just as children do.
  • Understanding emotions is an important first step to regulating one's reaction.
  • Suppressing emotions can increase distress; naming and validating them can help restore balance.

Before I had children, I thought it would be hard and fun. I expected to be tired. I expected to have less time for myself. But I never expected to be so challenged by the emotions I had, like guilt and anger. And I was not equipped with the knowledge, skills, and tools I needed to navigate my emotions as a parent.

The emotional lives of parents are complex and important, especially for mental health. That’s because parenting evokes some of our biggest and most complicated emotions.

For example:

  • You can adore your child and still feel furious when they refuse to get dressed.
  • You can feel deep gratitude and, five minutes later, feel overwhelmed, resentful, anxious, or exhausted.
  • You can know exactly how you want to respond to your child and then hear yourself saying something you wish you hadn’t said.
  • You can genuinely want to hear and understand your adult child, while still feeling defensive when they criticize you.

Having “negative” emotions towards children doesn’t mean we’re bad. It just means we have emotions, as all humans do. And contrary to what we may think, core emotions like anger, sadness, and fear are not under conscious control.

What does emotional regulation actually mean?

Emotional regulation refers to a calm and balanced nervous system. When we are regulated, we can experience our emotions, deal with them effectively, and relate in connected and attuned ways. When we are regulated, we don’t feel threatened by our children’s behaviors or emotions. Our capacity for compassion and curiosity is enabled—the qualities we need as parents.

Nevertheless, as parents, we are regularly thrown off balance because our children evoke strong feelings.

When I was young, I thought the only way to feel calmer was to get rid of my emotions by pushing them away or distracting myself. This is how many people think because we aren’t taught about emotions and how to be with them in healthy ways.

The goal isn’t to become a parent who never gets angry, frustrated, afraid, or overwhelmed. That’s simply not possible because emotions are hardwired into the brain and body and cannot be eradicated. Pushing emotions down dysregulates the nervous system, stressing the mind and body, which worsens anxiety and depression.

A better goal is to learn about emotions, develop emotional awareness, and ultimately learn how to process emotions. For example, being able to recognize and name the anger, fear, shame, sadness, or disappointment that you’re feeling begins the process of regulation, helping us feel and function better.

That’s a very different approach than ignoring your emotions and simply telling yourself to “calm down.”

  • You can feel angry without yelling.
  • You can feel anxious without becoming controlling.
  • You can feel resentful without punishing your child.
  • You can feel sad without shutting down.
  • You can feel disappointed without making your child feel guilty about disappointing you.

How do we learn this?

The Change Triangle: A roadmap for emotional regulation

One very effective way to understand and work with difficult emotions is through the Change Triangle, an emotional roadmap I adapted from AEDP psychotherapy and the academic literature on emotions.

Initially, the Change Triangle helps by teaching us the ABCs of emotions and how they work in the mind and body. As a result of this newfound emotional education, we can become less fearful of our emotions and more curious about what is happening inside us.

The Change Triangle Tool for Parents Shows the Path to Regulation
Source: Hilary Jacobs Hendel

When something upsets you, you can turn inward and find where you are on the Change Triangle. You will find yourself in one of four places on the Change Triangle.

  1. The top left of the Change Triangle is avoiding your emotions with protective defenses. Yelling, withdrawing, controlling, and drinking are just some of the many brilliant and creative ways we avoid dealing directly with our emotions.
  2. You may find yourself in the top right corner experiencing anxiety, guilt, or shame. These inhibitory emotions help push down our core emotions.
  3. You may have identified that you are experiencing one of the seven core emotions at the bottom corner of the Change Triangle.
  4. Or you may be feeling calm and balanced. This is a regulated state where we feel like this is me. We want to spend as much time as possible in this openhearted state of the authentic self.

Protective defenses and inhibitory emotions obscure deeper core emotions such as anger, sadness, fear, disgust, or joy. Naming and validating our core emotions opens the door to regulation. The ultimate objective whenever we get dysregulated is to work our way back down the Change Triangle, moving from defenses back to the openhearted state of the authentic self, which is a regulated state.

Next time you get upset, instead of immediately reacting, pause and ask yourself:

  • What am I feeling right now?
  • Where do I feel it in my body?
  • What is the emotion trying to tell me?
  • Is there another emotion or need that is deeper?

This kind of curiosity creates space between feeling and action. And that space can change how we parent.

What does emotional regulation look like in real life?

Imagine your eight-year-old refuses to turn off the television. You feel your body tighten. Your heart beats faster. You hear yourself thinking, Why won’t this kid ever listen to me?

You could yell: “Turn it off right now!”

Or you could pause.

You might notice: I’m really angry.

When you listen to the anger and get curious about why you’re angry and what you need, you might notice something underneath the anger: I’m exhausted. I feel powerless. I need cooperation.

The situation hasn’t magically changed. Your child still needs to turn off the television. But now you’re responding from greater awareness rather than simply discharging the emotion.

You can set the same boundary without making your child the target of your unprocessed feelings. That’s emotional regulation.

Instead of yelling, gently take the remote from your child, turn off the TV, and tell your child calmly, “TV time is over.”

Parents need emotional skills, too

We spend enormous amounts of time teaching children about their emotions. We tell them to use their words. We teach them to take deep breaths. We encourage them to name their feelings and calm down. But parents need these skills, too. In fact, one of the most powerful ways to teach children emotional intelligence is to develop our own emotional intelligence. When parents learn to understand and process their emotions, they become better able to help their children do the same.

item.title: Unblending: the IFS Approach to Learning
item.description:
Education

Unblending: the IFS Approach to Learning

To learn in therapy embrace uncertainty, pay attention, and let expectations go.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • We learn when we let experience contradict expectations.
  • We let experience contradict expectations when we feel safe enough to try something new.
  • We feel safe enough to try new things when we won’t be blamed for failing.
  • We don’t blame ourselves for failing when we feel lovable and loved.

Co-authored with Sarah Bergenfield

Artists, writers, and musicians shape experience and hold the interest of an audience by introducing things that are unresolved, promise resolution, and offer hints along the way. A crime novel asks whodunnit; music creates gripping tension and aesthetic chills; plays and movies pose and ponder problems; paintings invite, and so on. Artists know that we stay with what we do not yet understand and we feel thrilled at discovery.

The journey from not knowing to understanding by way of curiosity and exploration is called an epistemic arc. Sometimes we’re captured by a puzzle and we understand gradually, sometimes the epiphany comes quickly. In either case, that aha! moment signifies the soft thump of the tiny dopamine hit that culminates an exploration. But to reach this moment, we have to be open to our existing ideas about identity and relationships being incomplete.

Who Am I? Why Do I Think/Feel/Act This Way?

From the Internal Family Systems (IFS) perspective, we all have parts. We may see, hear, sense, or feel them. They present at different ages and, often, act in ways that don’t fit the current moment because they’re stuck in the past. When a part takes over and we see the world through its eyes, expecting what it expects, IFS says the part is blended. This can cause epochal (and often epical) cognitive confusion. Who am I? How old am I? Why do I think this way, feel this way, act this way? In contrast, when the part separates, or unblends, we can notice and relate to it. When we pay attention, parts unblend and we can get into relationship with them, ask what they fear, and meet their need for validation, connection, and love.

IFS therapy sessions follow the epistemic arc. Clients arrive in therapy puzzled by their behavior (Why do I pull away when I want connection?), but wedded to some familiar certainty, like I am bad, or no one can be trusted. The IFS inquiry invites them to be curious about their behavior and beliefs, which almost always leads to formative experiences.

The Epistemic Arc Begins with Unblending and Ends with Insight

The phenomena IFS calls blending and unblending illustrate a paradox at the heart of subjective experience. We can be a part or we can be with a part. When we are a part, we think, feel, and act like that part, but when we are with a part, we have choices. If, for example, a blended part expects rejection, we are likely to hear silence as rejection and view a later offer of help as untrustworthy or dangerous. The part is too afraid to try something new and our present remains a perpetual repetition of the past. But the opposite is true as well. If the part unblends and we are with it, we can explore its fear and challenge distorted and inaccurate beliefs. I can feel and hear a part that expects to be rejected, but since I’ll be okay whatever happens, I can afford to try something new.

How New Experiences Change Old Expectations

An IFS session follows an epistemic arc, a process we can understand through the lens of neuroscience and predictive processing, which says the brain builds a world model in childhood and then, conserving energy, predicts the familiar. Ideally, the brain updates its predictive model in response to prediction errors, but fear and negative identity beliefs can get in the way. A person who expects rejection and withdraws will not get a chance to learn how others might respond if they were to stay present and express a need.

From the predictive processing perspective, blended parts block the brain’s ability to learn. In contrast, unblending clears the runway. IFS aims to persuade parts to unblend. Our compassion and respect invite engagement, parts acknowledge us, and mutual curiosity sustains investigation. Once parts feel valid, legitimate, lovable, and connected, we feel—and are—more open to experiences that disconfirm old beliefs. Expectations relax, other information gains influence, and the brain’s world model updates.

An IFS inquiry doesn’t push for change. Pressing a part to step aside or move quickly can confirm an expectation that its wishes and limits will be disregarded. Patience conveys concern and respect, and is valuable in itself. The message to parts is: You can hesitate and stay connected. You can express fear and be heard. IFS invites all parts to take time exploring their fears and needs. Faster? Slower? You’re the boss.

IFS and Self-Help

If you want to discover the logic behind some apparently inexplicable behavior of your own, encourage your parts to unblend. Try noticing them and getting curious. You might have a protective part that keeps everyone happy because it expects disagreements to end relationships. Or you might have a part that withdraws because it anticipates unreasonable—or unmeetable—demands. Your protectors can explain the rationale for their beliefs and behaviors. Your job is to listen with an open heart.

As you listen, you can validate protective choices but also challenge negative identity conclusions (I’m worthless… something is wrong with me). You can offer to replace old survival tactics with better options. You don’t have to undo the past, convince transgressors to take it back, or prove your worth. The part you protect is valid, lovable, and—if you let me help—loved. Your protectors may need to move toward this invitation slowly, starting with a question they can now tolerate asking: Can things be different? But those aha! moments, when they come, are transformative.

item.title: Meta's Billions Won't Fix Youth Mental Health on Its Own
item.description:
Social Media

Meta's Billions Won't Fix Youth Mental Health on Its Own

How states can avoid costly mistakes and invest wisely in youth mental well-being.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • Meta settlement funds for platform designs that harmed youth won't solve the youth mental health crisis alone.
  • To meet the moment states must avoid opioid settlement mistakes through transparency and accountability.
  • Youth voices must help shape how settlement dollars are invested and evaluated.

If I had $17 billion dollars from Meta in the settlement of one social media addiction case, I know exactly what I would not do with it. I would not spend it the way states have been spending their opioid settlement money.

Over the past several years, tens of billions of dollars have flowed to states from opioid settlements meant to save lives through prevention, treatment, and recovery. While opioid-related deaths have declined, how much of that decline is attributable to settlement-funded initiatives is unclear. This is a fact researchers partly trace to the glacial pace of spending, fragmented efforts, and a lack of transparency.

Now, states face a smaller-scale version of the same test, this time over youth and social media. In late August, Meta agreed to pay $12.1 billion to resolve a lawsuit brought by 47 states and the District of Columbia that claimed Facebook and Instagram were designed to hook young users at the expense of their mental health. A chunk of that money is earmarked for youth online safety and mental health initiatives and will be paid out over the next ten years, pending court approval. Meta is dangling an additional $5 billion if other major platforms match the restrictions in the settlement.

Meta agreed to numerous product changes, including stronger age verification, parental controls, and an end to overnight use. But few states are relying on that alone, taking matters into their own hands. California, for example, passed bipartisan legislation on September 20th, 2026, banning infinite scrolling and personalized algorithmic feeds for youth under 16.

That said, as a clinical psychologist, Yale professor, and youth mental health expert, I know the devil is in the details, not the celebratory headlines. What gets done with this money, and how quickly, is still an open question. But if states take a few real notes from the opioid settlement, they can handle this one differently.

First, we have to get real. The Meta settlement was an important exercise in accountability for technology companies, but this money will not solve the youth mental health crisis. It can't. Social media is only one thread of a much larger knot of problems affecting youth mental health. While Meta plays a role here, it is our collective responsibility to improve equity in mental health support availability, access, and quality.

Second, one of the clearest critiques of the opioid settlements is the absence of any national requirement that states report where they spend the money. At a minimum, every state receiving Meta settlement funds should publicly share what it funds, what it's learning, and what isn't working, on a recurring timeline. Minnesota runs a public dashboard breaking down settlement spending, and North Carolina requires local governments to report spending annually through a public portal. Beyond spending transparency, with different amounts per state, implementation and outcomes transparency is also key. California, which helped lead the case, stands to receive the largest final payout, in excess of $2 billion. That puts California and other large recipient states in a position to share their implementation strategies, pilot data, and model resources that other states with smaller amounts can use.

States must also be disciplined. With healthcare budgets under pressure from federal Medicaid changes, especially for access to mental health services, the temptation to backfill budget holes is understandable. But this approach is unlikely to produce sustainable change. Even the roughly $56 billion states and localities receiving over 18 years in opioid settlements doesn't come close to covering what's been lost elsewhere, according to published analyses from the Bipartisan Policy Center’s Opioid Crisis Task Force. This money was never going to replace existing investment, only add to it. That's why at least a dozen states have written explicit restrictions into law against using opioid settlement funds to backfill existing budgets, and states handling the Meta settlement should adopt that restriction from day one.

Finally (for now), young people must be included in whatever gets built on their behalf from these dollars. Their lived experience is vital expertise, and its absence is a documented missed opportunity in the opioid settlements. According to reports, only about 7 percent of people on opioid settlement advisory committees nationally had lived experience for the crisis they were advising on. Alternatively, Washington state required at least four members with lived experience to be appointed members to the settlement committee and compensated for their work. States building out Meta settlement advisory structures should build from this model. Implementation of any solutions is certain to be more successful when young people, their communities, and priorities are centered.

I don't have $12 billion settlement dollars, and neither does any single state on its own. But every state that's about to receive a piece of this Meta settlement has more control over what happens next than the opioid settlements ever gave states credit for exercising. The difference this time isn't the dollar amount. It's whether we treat the last decade of settlement spending as a cautionary tale or as a blueprint we already have in hand.

item.title: How Gossip Is Good for Us
item.description:
Social Life

How Gossip Is Good for Us

Sharing stories through gossip helps maintain social cohesion.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • Gossip has a long evolutionary history in maintaining social groups.
  • Gossip is adaptive in providing advice and life lessons.
  • Although gossip can sometimes be damaging, the positive benefits outweigh the negative.

As the saying goes, “If you don’t have anything good to say, don’t say anything.” But in the words of Alice Roosevelt Longworth, perhaps more of us prefer: “If you can’t say something good about someone, sit right here by me.” After all, deep down, we all love some good gossip, don’t we?

In fact, by some estimates of everyday conversations, upwards of 65 percent of what we talk about involves people and social interactions, both self-disclosures and information about others’ escapades. And “gossip,” defined as the telling of stories about the everyday adventures of the people in our lives that we tell to, with, and about others, began deep in our evolutionary history. As soon as we began to use language, we started to gossip!

As we gather around the holiday table this year with friends and family we may not have seen in a while, we will share stories of our lives, stories of their lives, and stories of our friends and family not able to be present at the table. The good news is that this is actually good for us. Whereas gossip has a bad reputation, in fact, it serves a critical function in weaving our lives together and keeping our social groups connected.

Dunbar, an evolutionary anthropologist, argues that gossip began very early in our ancestral history. Living in larger social groups benefited our survival, and gossip is a necessary part of keeping larger social groups cohesive. Through sharing stories about how Uncle Joe and Aunt Louise are settling into their new living arrangements in Timbuktu, we maintain a sense of belonging to the group, and this sense of belonging adds to our own sense of meaning and purpose in life. When we feel socially isolated, we actually experience physical pain; Williams and Nida show experimentally that social exclusion for as little as two minutes leads to physiological pain responses and emotional distress, and longer periods of social isolation can result in depression, helplessness, and alienation. Maintaining social connections by integrating our lives with others through stories and gossip brings us together and creates a sense of well-being.

Gossip also serves to help us with advice and discussion of possible problems—if you are thinking about changing jobs, a story about cousin Bill who just did that could provide invaluable information as you consider your options. With my colleagues David Pillemer and Dorthe Thomsen, we showed how these kinds of vicarious stories, stories about other people that resonate with who we are, can promote successful adaptation, help us make good decisions, and teach us morals and values for how to live a good life. We don’t have to experience things directly to learn from them. We can learn from the experiences of others through gossip.

Vicarious stories are particularly prominent in family storytelling. Alongside stories of shared family experiences, such as the Thanksgiving when Dad dropped the turkey on the kitchen floor, and we all had to eat hot dogs, are stories of the family past: stories about parents growing up or grandparents, aunts, and uncles. When the younger generation hears these stories, whether from the person who experienced them (“When I was your age….”) or third-hand as gossip (“Your grandfather loved Thanksgiving, and every year, he would invite friends from work who had nowhere else to go”), these stories become frameworks for how to live a life. Gossip provides us with maps for how the world works.

Of course, there is a dark side to gossip. As Dores-Cruz and colleagues point out, gossip can be used to purposely damage someone else’s reputation, perhaps in the service of self-aggrandizement, and thus can lead to mistrust within the group. They conducted a series of studies to assess people’s motivations and tendency to gossip, especially when the person being gossiped about was experimentally manipulated to be a victim of malicious rumors. They found that group members were more likely to gossip when a group member was being maliciously maligned in order to protect the victim’s reputation. At the same time, people are motivated to spread the word about members of the group who violate norms, suggesting that gossip serves to keep everyone in line. Gossip is a little bit like herding sheep, making sure the group maintains positive bonds and bringing those who deviate from this back into the fold.

This holiday season, there will be gossip! I will spend Thanksgiving with my “framily” (friends and family), and there will be some dear framily we will miss who are not able to be there. But we will gossip! “Did you hear about so-and-so?” and “Let me tell you what happened…” We will laugh, and we will shed tears. And we will cement our bonds. So, this Thanksgiving, if you have something juicy to tell, come sit by me!

item.title: What the Recent Tech Outage Can Teach Us About Balance
item.description:
Burnout

What the Recent Tech Outage Can Teach Us About Balance

A widespread inconvenience can actually be an opportunity to slow down.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • A widespread tech outage can remind us of the importance of work-life balance.
  • As rates of burnout rise, a willingness to create healthy work habits is more important than ever.
  • This unexpected inconvenience can offer an opportunity to allow ourselves to slow down.

As I write this, parts of North America and Europe are experiencing a Microsoft outage that is affecting certain parts of the cloud infrastructure, particularly office communication services such as Outlook, Teams, and Microsoft 360. While this is certainly causing disruption and inconvenience in many corporate and business settings, it may also be reminding us of an important reality that we often talk about but rarely implement: work-life balance.

In the United States, it has long been reported that workers struggle with creating healthy boundaries between their lives and their jobs, and a 2025 study found that a staggering 66 percent of American workers reported having experienced “some degree of burnout” in the past year (Robinson, 2025). Additionally, 2024 research indicated that 44 percent of employees and 53 percent of supervisors experienced burnout at their jobs (Malinsky, 2022). It is no secret that many of us struggle to find the “sweet spot” between work and the rest of our lives. Increasingly, this disparity between work and life is being seen as a larger problem that, according to a 2021 study, is more than “an individual-level phenomenon,” and is “a societal concern that necessitates systematic support from a wider range of stakeholders” (Fan, Yuyang, et al., 2021).

Along with the statistical evidence, we can find plenty of anecdotal proof that this is a widespread problem: you would be hard-pressed to find a person who does not report some level of exhaustion or burnout related to their career, myself and those I know being no exception. But if it is such an issue, why are we unable to see something like this Microsoft outage as a gift rather than an inconvenience? I would argue that it has to do with our longstanding relationship with work and our misprioritization of its importance. American attitudes about work have long been centered around productivity, busyness, results, and multitasking. Words like “balance” are simply not part of our career-related vernacular.

When something like a technology outage forces us to let go of our usual outcome-orientation towards our jobs, it can feel odd and somehow “wrong.” Looking at social media comments today, I am seeing more that speak to how annoying and inconvenient this outage is and less that speak to it allowing for a slower workday or an (albeit forced) opportunity to not work as hard. But perhaps we can learn from today’s widespread inconvenience. In some workplaces, you are unable to send or answer emails, communicate as usual, or access cloud-related platforms. In one sense, this is frustrating. In another, it is permission not to do these things that, let’s be honest, are often done from home, from the dinner table, at unhealthy hours, in the midst of other life activities, and at the cost of mindfulness and presence in our lives. I am not suggesting that tech outages are good for business, but rather that they can remind us that creating space between work and life is necessary for our overall well-being.

Sometimes inconveniences can be opportunities. In Buddhist philosophy, the concept that the “obstacle is the path” is applicable to today’s inconvenience. The obstacle (not being able to access the usual work platforms) is the path to allowing ourselves to slow down and create some space between work and life—at least for a day or two.

item.title: DARVO at Work: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

DARVO at Work: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender

How people who speak up are labeled The Problem, and how to stick to your truth.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • DARVO stands for deny, attack, and reverse victim and offender, a common response to being held accountable.
  • DARVO makes observers doubt the person who raised the concern. It can also make that person doubt themselves.
  • Learning to recognize the pattern weakens its effect.
  • Sticking to the original question can counteract the effects of DARVO.
Source: Tookapic / Pexels

Simone had done everything right. She had led her department's most impactful projects, trained half the team, and been told twice that she was "next in line" for a senior manager role.

Then the promotion went to Mark. He had been with the company for about a year, created extra work for others by turning in slop, and, as nearly everyone knew, had been in a relationship with their boss, Jody, for the last 6 months.

Simone didn't accuse anyone of anything. She politely asked HR whether the promotion process had been reviewed for a conflict of interest. Before long, Simone was labeled "a troublemaker," and somehow Jody was a victim of "harassment about her private life."

How does the person who raised a legitimate concern end up as the problem, while the person who created the problem ends up as the victim?

DARVO: Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender

Jennifer Freyd (1997) coined the term DARVO— for Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender—to describe how people often respond when confronted about wrongdoing. It was first studied in the context of domestic violence and abuse, but it occurs anywhere accountability is brought up, including the workplace.

The pattern has three moves:

  • Deny. "Nothing happened." "There is no conflict of interest." "Ridiculous."
  • Attack. Shift focus to the person who raised the question, their “tone,” motives, competence, or character.
  • Reverse Victim and Offender. Claim that you are the one being harmed by questioning, “witch hunt,” or jealousy.

DARVO can be deliberate and calculated, or reflexive and emotion-driven. Either way, the person who dared to speak up is vilified. Here’s how it might have played out with Simone and Jody.

  • Deny. When HR asks Jody about the promotion, she insists that the decision was "purely merit-based." Her relationship with Mark doesn't exist (outright denial) or is "irrelevant" and “nobody's business.”
  • Attack. The focus moves from the decision to the person who questioned it. Simone is "bitter” and "spreading rumors." Jody insists Simone "has always been difficult." The sneaky switch is that the question Was this promotion fair? has been replaced by the question What's wrong with Simone?
  • Reverse Victim and Offender. In classic DARVO, Jody becomes the injured party. She complains that she feels "harassed" and that her privacy has been violated. Mark says he's being bullied by people who resent his success.

DARVO accomplished.

The organization's attention switches to protecting Jody and Mark, the people with power, and away from advocating for Simone, someone originally harmed by that power. And the original concern, a manager granting a promotion to her lover in violation of conflict-of-interest policy, has disappeared from the conversation. It’s now about "You are attacking my private life and hurting my feelings."

Does DARVO Work?

DARVO is used so often because it is effective. Research shows it. In a 2020 set of experiments, people read the same incident with or without the accused person's DARVO response. When DARVO was present, readers judged the victim as less believable and more to blame, and the perpetrator as less responsible (Harsey & Freyd, 2020).

DARVO can also gaslight the original target. Harsey, Zurbriggen, and Freyd (2017) found that the more DARVO people encountered when confronting someone who had wronged them, the more they blamed themselves. Self-blame can lead to self-silencing, and Simone might come to wonder if she really is "just bitter" and should say nothing.

From the inside, DARVO can spur confusion. Simone starts editing her own memory: Was her tone too sharp? Did she misread something? Was she, deep down, just jealous? Each doubt could make sense, and that’s what makes them dangerous. Over time, that self-doubt can harden into silence—a coping strategy that may cost you who you are. So, if you find yourself wondering whether you were the problem, keep asking yourself: What actually happened first?

Resisting DARVO

Research also offers some good news: People who were taught to recognize the DARVO pattern were less swayed by it. They saw the victim as more credible and the perpetrator as less so. Simply knowing the pattern's name weakens its grip (Harsey & Freyd, 2020). Of course, recognizing the pattern requires paying attention. The clearest signal is a subject change. If a question about a decision turns into complaints about the questioner's tone, personality, or propriety, ask why.

If you're the target:

  • Name the pattern, at least to yourself. Self-blame is part of how DARVO works.
  • Keep returning to the original issue. "My question is whether the promotion process was reviewed for a conflict of interest."
  • Document dates, decisions, and what was said, in writing.
  • Look for allies and, if needed, outside advice. In many jurisdictions, retaliation for raising a good-faith concern may have legal consequences.

If you're a bystander:

  • Don't repeat the "difficult employee" story without evidence.
  • Ask the neutral question out loud: "Was the conflict of interest ever addressed?"
  • Tell the target what you saw. Being believed by even one person can make all the difference.

If you're a leader or HR representative:

  • Separate the issues. A counter-complaint does not cancel the original concern; investigate the decision first.
  • Watch for timing. Negative feedback that appears only after someone speaks up is a red flag for retaliation.
  • Teach investigators to recognize DARVO.

DARVO succeeds by making us forget the original question. In Simone's case, it was simple: Was there a conflict of interest? Everything that followed—the denials, the attacks on Simone, Jody's claims of being a victim—was meant to bury it.

Do not be distracted. Hold on to the original concern. Keep asking “what happened first.” And insist on the resolution of the original question.

If you need sample scripts, here are some options:

If you’re the target:

  • “I’m glad to discuss that separately. Can we address the original question first?”
  • “My question remains: Was the promotion reviewed for a conflict of interest?”
  • “I understand this is uncomfortable. I still need an answer to what I raised.”

If you’re a bystander:

  • “Wait, did we ever resolve the conflict-of-interest question?”
  • “Before we talk about Simone, what happened with the promotion?”

If you're a leader or HR representative:

  • “We’ll look into that complaint. The original concern comes first.”

DARVO depends on changing the subject. These phrases change it back.

An early version of this post appeared in the Best Work for Your Brain newsletter.

item.title: Two Sides of Human Nature: Why We Become Angels or Devils
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Two Sides of Human Nature: Why We Become Angels or Devils

Do conditions determine whether we are more human or behave more instinctively?

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • The brain’s main function becomes making instinctive choices aimed at survival.
  • However, human nature encompasses both instinctive drives and higher moral capacities.
  • The prefrontal cortex may be what makes us more human.
  • The harsh conditions and subsequent stress may shape behaviors now considered selfish or aggressive.

Many countries and regions are affected by war, violence, and social unrest in the world. These regions typically also face extremely serious living and economic conditions. Conversely, in richer nations with more favorable conditions, people adhere more closely to ethical standards, the law, and human principles. A prime example is the countries of Northern Europe, which experience lower rates of crime and political unrest than many other nations and consistently rank among the happiest in the world [1]. It is striking that these countries, due to harsh climatic conditions and difficult access to resources, have at times had a history marked entirely by war, violence, and malevolence.

Dual nature of humans

The dual nature of human beings has been a subject of religion, mysticism, philosophy, and ethics throughout history. These schools of thought have acknowledged an animalistic dimension—characterized by malice, selfishness, deceit, envy, violence, and greed—alongside a dimension that aspires toward transcendence, defined by generosity, kindness, and self-sacrifice. At times, individuals may even surrender their own lives—the most fundamental instinct of all living creatures—for others or higher values. Religious traditions attribute the root of this duality to the unique creation of the human species. From this perspective, humans, like other animals, possess a physical body rooted in the Earth, driven by an instinctive desire for survival and a craving to secure greater access to food, water, and warm, safe shelter protected from predators.

The lives of our ancestors were largely spent in harsh and unforgiving environments, where survival was naturally the main priority. This response is also observed in many other animals. Much of what we now classify as moral vices actually consisted of behaviors aimed at individual survival and the acquisition of resources. However, in less hostile conditions—and when well-fed and at peace—humans become tamer; they begin to attend to the needs and suffering of others, prioritizing family and tribe but extending concern even to more distant fellow human beings. In such a state, humans develop a desire to understand the world, engage in artistic creation, and reflect on the universe around them.

Religions offer precepts and rituals to bring the animalistic nature under control and allow the transcendent dimension to flourish. Yet the malevolent aspect of human nature has, at times, even exploited religion to serve selfish, animalistic desires. Throughout history, countless wars and acts of bloodshed have unfolded under the guise of religion.

Does the origin of human duality lie in the brain?

For centuries, humans have considered themselves superior to other living beings due to their intelligence. However, a systematic review has shown that many abilities once thought to be “uniquely human”—such as tool-making, planning, and problem-solving—are also present, to some extent, in other animals. Nevertheless, humans exhibit exceptionally strong capabilities in areas such as recalling the past and imagining the future, tool use, problem-solving, social cognition, and communication. No single trait exclusive to humans can account for this superiority; this applies even to distinct capacities like language. We do not possess a single “magical” trait, nor has culture alone shaped us. Rather, our abilities reinforce one another—a synergy evident in both child development and the co-evolution of genes and culture [2].

It appears that the root of human superiority and behavior originates largely from the human brain’s larger and more complex cerebral cortex. The structure and genetics of this brain region are distinctly different from those of our close primate relatives, such as chimpanzees; they also exhibit significant differences compared to Neanderthals and even our own ancestors from thousands of years ago. This enables our species—through the expansion of collective culture—to obtain a more distinctly human standard for living. However, this region does not always exert complete control over the lower brain centers responsible for governing vital instincts (3).

When we are hungry, exposed to freezing conditions, have failed in competition for a mate, or face the threat of predation by animals or other humans, our sympathetic nervous system—the “fight-or-flight” mechanism—is instinctively activated. This system triggers metabolic changes to supply necessary fuel, modulates the immune system to combat infections and physical injuries, and induces cardiovascular responses to help us cope with these conditions. Psychologically, it generates stress and anxiety, activating specific brain regions such as the amygdala.

The amygdala disrupts the interaction between the higher brain centers—the neocortex—and the lower, more primitive structures. Consequently, the brain shifts toward rapid, instinctive decision-making, bypassing the slower, more deliberate, and effortful processes of reflection. In this state, an individual temporarily loses the capacity for analytical thinking and self-critique; instead, the brain’s primary function becomes making instinctive choices aimed at survival. Under these circumstances, moral priorities fade into the background [4].

However, given recent advancements in neuroscience, dividing the brain into “higher” human regions and “lower” animalistic ones is an oversimplification. In 1960, Paul D. MacLean proposed the “triune brain” theory—three distinct components: the reptilian brain, the limbic system, and the neocortex. He attributed instinctive behaviors like territoriality, dominance, mating, and deception primarily to the reptilian brain, suggesting these components operate largely independently.

In recent decades, however, this theory has faced significant criticism. We now understand the brain as an interconnected network, not a collection of independent layers. Emotions and cognition are deeply intertwined, and no single region can be considered solely responsible for any complex behavior [5].

When welfare becomes a weapon used against people

Human beings possess remarkable capacities for cooperation, compassion, and creativity, as well as powerful tendencies toward self-preservation, competition, and aggression. Which of these tendencies becomes dominant depends not only on our evolutionary heritage and brain organization but also on the psychological, social, and environmental conditions in which we live. Harsh conditions often breed greater violence and depravity, potentially turning affected societies into a “geopolitical ulcer” that creates challenges for other nations as well. Such circumstances may also drive individuals toward misery, crime, and lawlessness.

Furthermore, the political strategies of powerful countries—which undermine the welfare, education, healthcare, and housing of targeted nations—can distort the human values within those communities. Ultimately, these actions will return to haunt the perpetrators, much like a boomerang. Still, cruelty does not always arise from bad conditions; sometimes dangerous beliefs, using our finest mental capacities, can produce violence and chaos even in comfortable circumstances.

item.title: How to Make Retirement the Best Time of Your Life
item.description:
Aging

How to Make Retirement the Best Time of Your Life

Celebrating the freedom to choose how to spend your time.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • Retirement is more than staying busy; it's about becoming fulfilled.
  • Freedom of choice mediates post-employment satisfaction.
  • Selecting social groups based on enjoyment boosts life satisfaction.

The word “retirement” evokes different imagery for different people. Some envision lounging on the beach with a cool drink; others are excited to finally apply for the job they always wanted. Then there are those who are unprepared to suddenly face free time, often for the first time in their lives, which can provoke anxiety as well as anticipation. Yet for everyone nearing the end of a career, one important contributor to a happy, healthy retirement is the freedom to choose how to spend your time. Research explains.

Source: Image by Mana Obed from Pixabay

Finally Free: Choosing How to Spend Time

As I explored in more detail in a previous post,[i] Anastasia Fadeeva et al. (2025) investigated the interplay between individual and contextual factors in seeking to understand the framework within which people experience and navigate retirement.[ii] They identified three prominent themes: rebuilding identity, social interaction, and independence. Regarding identity, they note that many of their retired study participants experienced an identity crisis because of having lost their role at work, which is consistent with the link between retirement and identity transition, including the quest for new meaning in life. Fadeeva et al. reported that their study participants attempted to incorporate new roles and activities, reinforce other spheres of life, or revive former interests or habits. Yet unfortunately, because not every activity provides new meaning, many recent retirees continually search for fulfilling and satisfying pursuits.

Fadeeva et al. do, however, highlight the value of breaking free from a work routine, sometimes referred to by recent retirees as the “honeymoon” phase, which makes sense considering the most anticipated factor for this group is freedom from work stress and obligations. Yet other research indicates the key to happiness post-retirement may be choosing group affiliation that is positive and fulfilling.

More Than “Staying Busy:” Socialize Strategically

One key to post-employment fulfillment is affiliation with several types of social groups instead of maintaining a single source of identity. Catherine Haslam et al. (2023)[iii] found that different types of social factors contribute to successful transition into retirement. Studying a sample of Australian workers who had retired within the past year, they found that although pre-retirement group memberships did not directly impact retirement outcomes directly, they served as sources of support by allowing retirees to maintain existing group memberships while gaining new ones. Their findings confirmed the significance of social dynamics and group membership for the health and well-being of retirees.

Yet other research validates what many ex-employees have experienced first-hand: not all post-retirement social group memberships are equally fulfilling. Crystal J. La Rue et al. (2024)[iv] found that group memberships that are important and supportive prompt better adjustment in retirement. Using data from 489 retirees who belonged to 1887 groups, they found that retirees who belonged to more optimal groups enjoyed better adjustment, higher life satisfaction and mental health outcomes, while belonging to groups described as ambivalent or straining (including experiencing some degree of rejection) contributed to poorer adjustment, lower life satisfaction and a higher degree of depression.

Because most of us already know what type of affiliations bring us the most pleasure, research confirms those should take priority. From faith to family, fitness to philanthropy, the key is freedom of choice. Living our best lives post-employment is not about staying busy but staying fulfilled—which could make retirement the best years of your life.

item.title: Why Can’t I Stop Over-Drinking on My Own?
item.description:
Alcoholism

Why Can’t I Stop Over-Drinking on My Own?

Willpower alone is often not enough to overcome a long-standing alcohol problem.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • Willpower alone is often insufficient to overcome deeply ingrained patterns of excessive drinking.
  • Repeated heavy drinking can alter brain chemistry, making alcohol use increasingly automatic.
  • Alcohol's ability to relieve emotional distress can powerfully reinforce continued drinking.
  • Professional treatment and medication can help interrupt persistent, self-destructive drinking patterns.

“Why can’t I get my drinking under control? I know I’m drinking too much. I’ve promised myself countless times that I’ll cut back or stop altogether, but sooner or later I end up doing the same thing again.”

I’ve heard some version of this question thousands of times during my 50-plus years of clinical practice as an addiction psychologist. Many are high-functioning individuals capable of exercising considerable discipline and self-control in other areas of their lives. Yet when it comes to drinking, they repeatedly fail to follow through on their intentions.

Why does this happen? And why do some people find it so difficult to change their drinking habits without professional help and/or medication?

Wanting to Change Isn’t the Same as Being Able to Change

Consider someone who wakes up after a night of heavy drinking feeling miserable, embarrassed, and absolutely determined never to repeat the experience. Several days later, however, after a stressful workday or during a social gathering, having a few drinks once again seems innocuous. Yesterday’s determination is displaced by other motivations, some operating outside conscious awareness.

Consider the case of a successful businessman who sought my help several months ago after a series of alcohol-related incidents. Two years earlier, he had lost a highly coveted executive position after behaving inappropriately while intoxicated at a company function. Devastated by the experience, he stopped drinking and vowed never again to jeopardize his career. Regrettably, several months later, having secured another desirable position, he attended a business dinner followed by several hours of heavy drinking with co-workers at an after-hours club. Despite his earlier resolve and the painful consequences of his previous drinking, he again became severely intoxicated and behaved in ways that once more put his professional standing at risk.

How could someone who had already paid such a steep price repeat essentially the same behavior? This is precisely why I titled my first book on addiction treatment, published in 1989, Willpower’s Not Enough. Overcoming a deeply ingrained addictive behavior usually requires more than determination, good intentions, and repeated promises to oneself.

The Invisible Changes in Brain Chemistry

Repeated exposure to alcohol and other psychoactive drugs can gradually change the way the brain functions. These changes involve neural mechanisms responsible for reward, motivation, stress regulation, learning, and self-control. With repeated heavy drinking, the brain can develop a neurochemical relationship with alcohol that makes continued drinking increasingly compelling, even when the person desperately wants to stop.

Drinking can begin to operate on something resembling “autopilot,” no longer responding reliably to conscious intentions or rational consideration of its consequences. What initially served a pleasurable or useful purpose becomes a self-perpetuating pattern that continues despite destructive consequences. The behavior has become maladaptive, even self-sabotaging.

Drinking Becomes a Learned, Automatic Response

Over time, drinking becomes associated with particular situations, emotions, and expectations. Arriving home after work, walking into a favorite restaurant, or feeling anxious or upset may automatically trigger the thought that drinking would make everything feel better. These associations become stronger with repetition. Eventually, the urge to drink may arise before the person has consciously considered whether drinking is a good idea and what the potential consequences could be.

Another complication arises from the fact that alcohol itself impairs judgment and volitional control. Someone who fully intends to have only two drinks may find that, after consuming them, a third or fourth seems perfectly reasonable. The very substance they are trying to control interferes with their ability to control it. A person’s intention and determination not to overdrink can quickly dissolve in alcohol.

Alcohol as Self-Medication: When Relief Becomes Reinforcement

For many people, drinking serves an important “self-medication” function. It provides temporary relief from anxiety, depression, loneliness, anger, and other uncomfortable emotional states. It may also attenuate intrusive thoughts, persistent worry, or relentless self-criticism.

Alcohol’s ability to relieve or anesthetize psychological discomfort can make it especially difficult to give up. Drinking is no longer simply about enjoying a pleasant experience. It becomes a way of escaping an unpleasant one. This can multiply alcohol’s reinforcing value.

For someone who depends on alcohol to manage emotional discomfort, giving it up may feel like losing an important coping mechanism, even when drinking has become a serious problem. The irony is that excessive drinking often worsens the very symptoms it temporarily relieves. The result can be a vicious cycle in which drinking provides short-term relief while contributing to the conditions that make further drinking more likely.

When Repeated Failures Become Part of the Problem

Repeated unsuccessful attempts to control drinking can gradually erode a person’s confidence and motivation. Each episode of excessive drinking re-activates feelings of regret, self-criticism, and promises to do better next time. Eventually, some people begin to believe they are incapable of changing. I’ve seen this happen many times, particularly among high-functioning executives and professionals accustomed to solving problems through hard work, discipline, and persistence. They find it difficult to understand why those same qualities haven’t enabled them to overcome their drinking problem.

What Professional Help and Medication Can Accomplish

Treatment offers more than encouragement to exercise greater self-control. It helps identify the psychological, behavioral, and biological factors that keep excessive drinking going. This may involve recognizing situations that trigger drinking, interrupting automatic responses, developing alternative ways of managing emotional distress, and acquiring practical strategies for dealing with urges and setbacks.

For some, medication can make a substantial difference. FDA-approved medications such as naltrexone and disulfiram can help reduce drinking or support abstinence, depending on the medication and treatment goals. GLP-1 medications, such as semaglutide (Ozempic or Wegovy) and tirzepetide (Mounjaro or Zepbound), appear to be especially promising based on emerging research and clinical experience, although these drugs are not currently FDA-approved for treating alcohol use disorder.

Not everyone who drinks excessively needs professional treatment or medication. Some people successfully change on their own. Others benefit from brief guidance, while some require more sustained treatment. Nor does seeking treatment necessarily mean committing to lifelong abstinence. For some people, abstinence is clearly the safest and most realistic goal. For others, a harm reduction approach that supports learning to consistently moderate drinking may be possible.

A Better Question to Ask

When someone asks me, “Why can’t I overcome this problem on my own?” I often suggest a different question: What is it about my drinking that I haven’t yet understood or learned how to change? The issue isn’t necessarily a lack of motivation, intelligence, or strength of character. Years of repeated drinking may have established psychological habits and neurobiological changes that are difficult to reverse through determination alone.

Willpower certainly matters. But when addictive behavior has acquired a momentum of its own, willpower alone may not be enough to change its course.
