item.title: Do You Have Signs of 'Nomophobia'
item.description:
Fear

Do You Have Signs of 'Nomophobia'

The fear of being without a smartphone.

Posted November 13, 2026

Source: Sergey Meshkov / Pexels

What would your life be like without a smartphone? Some people may envision a peaceful life without distraction, and some may see a life with less convenience and connection.

Others, however, are terrified of the idea. Research has uncovered a new fear: “nomophobia.” Individuals become filled with dread, anxiety, and panic at the thought of being without their smartphone.

To measure the severity of this phobia and its effects on daily life, researchers have developed a test designed to assess and diagnose nomophobia. This tool not only examines the prevalence of this modern anxiety, but also prompts a broader discussion about our dependence on technology and its implications for mental well-being.

What Is Nomophobia?

Research defines nomophobia, no mobile phone phobia, as the fear of being detached from smartphone connectivity. While it is not a legitimate mental disorder like other specific phobias—such as fears of animals, storms, heights, and others—nomophobia’s conceptualization is founded on definitions from the Diagnostic Manual of Mental Disorders.

The research outlines that symptoms of nomophobia include many of those seen in other specific phobias, such as anxiety, shaking, sweating, agitation, and breathing difficulties. It was also found that those with low self-esteem and extraversion may be more prone to the overuse of smartphones, and therefore more likely to experience nomophobia.

According to one study, which aimed to review global statistics on the prevalence of the phobia, approximately 21 percent of the adult population suffers from severe nomophobia, and around 71 percent of the population has moderate nomophobia. The researchers found that college and university students seem most affected, with an alarming 25 percent prevalence.

Dealing with nomophobia can be challenging, given how ubiquitous smartphones are in modern life. The constant connectivity they provide has become integral to daily routines, making the mere thought of separation a source of intense anxiety for many. This not only induces immediate emotional distress, but can also contribute to long-term psychological effects that could affect overall well-being.

How to Know If You Have Nomophobia

The prevalence of nomophobia suggests a broader societal shift towards technology dependency, raising questions about the potential consequences for mental health.

As modern problems require modern solutions, a study in the journal Computers and Human Behavior sought to resolve the need to identify and address this. Through their research, they developed and validated a questionnaire to diagnose nomophobia. To use this self-report measure, individuals rate each statement on a scale from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree.”

  1. I would feel uncomfortable without constant access to information through my smartphone.
  2. I would be annoyed if I could not look up information on my smartphone when I wanted to do so.
  3. Being unable to get the news (happenings, weather, and so on) on my smartphone would make me nervous.
  4. I would be annoyed if I could not use my smartphone and/or its capabilities when I wanted to do so.
  5. Running out of battery in my smartphone would scare me.
  6. If I were to run out of credits or hit my monthly data limit, I would panic.
  7. If I did not have a data signal or could not connect to Wi-Fi, then I would constantly check to see if I had a signal or could find a Wi-Fi network.
  8. If I could not use my smartphone, I would be afraid of getting stranded somewhere.
  9. If I could not check my smartphone for a while, I would feel a desire to check it.

If I did not have my smartphone with me:

  1. I would feel anxious because I could not instantly communicate with my family and/or friends.
  2. I would be worried because my family and/or friends could not reach me.
  3. I would feel nervous because I would not be able to receive text messages and calls.
  4. I would be anxious because I could not keep in touch with my family and/or friends.
  5. I would be nervous because I could not know if someone had tried to reach me.
  6. I would feel anxious because my constant connection to my family and friends would be broken.
  7. I would be nervous because I would be disconnected from my online identity.
  8. I would be uncomfortable because I could not stay up to date with social media and online networks.
  9. I would feel awkward because I could not check my notifications for updates from my connections and online networks.
  10. I would feel anxious because I could not check my email messages.
  11. I would feel weird because I would not know what to do.

The questionnaire covers four different fear factors of nomophobia: inability to communicate, loss of connection, inaccessibility to information, and giving up convenience. Recognizing these patterns could be the first step toward a healthier relationship with technology and a better understanding of one’s own digital habits.

Identifying and addressing nomophobia is crucial—not only for our own mental health, but also for society at large. Take a moment to reflect on these statements and assess your feelings towards smartphone usage. Understanding the intricacies of your relationship with technology can empower you to make informed decisions and, if necessary, seek support in managing nomophobia. In a world where constant connectivity is the norm, taking time to evaluate the impact of this dependence can be a crucial aspect of maintaining your mental well-being.

item.title: Building Employee Resilience in Your Workplace
item.description:
Resilience

Building Employee Resilience in Your Workplace

An interview with I-O psychology expert Danielle King Jordan

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • Taking time to nurture close relationships and engage in mutual support helps people to be resilient.
  • Emotion regulation and moments of joy help us deal with the understandable feelings that come after adversity.
  • Rest and recovery are critical for having and using the energy that resilience requires.
  • Leaders can proactively interrogate whether a stressor can itself be addressed or removed.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

In an era marked by broad economic uncertainty, mass layoffs, and high cost of living, a focus on resilience in the workplace has become paramount. What can employers do to foster employee resilience in the workplace? To answer this question, I reached out to Danielle King Jordan, a Professor of Industrial-Organizational Psychology and the Founder and Principal Investigator of the WorKing Resilience Research Lab at Rice University. Her research focuses on employee resilience and stigma, and organizational resources that support employee thriving. I asked Danielle what I think are the four most important questions to help guide employers as they seek to foster employee resilience in the workplace.

JP: How should employers think about investing resources into employee resilience?

DKJ: There are three main approaches I would advocate for employers who want to support employee resilience: First, organizational decision-makers should look at problems, challenges, and adversities as an opportunity to support employees, not as a time to “test” resilience. Offering both proactive (before adversity) and reactive (throughout and after adversity) sources of support is ideal. What these resources look like depends on the types of adversity and on employee needs, so listening to your team is critical.

Second, before enacting resilience interventions, leaders can interrogate whether the adversity or challenge can itself be reduced or removed. This is the greatest source of support for future resilience to unavoidable issues. This is part of an adaptive, rather than a maladaptive, approach to resilience that we talk about in research.

And lastly, it is valuable to understand that we do not all experience adversity in the same way, so we should be willing to take a tailored, rather than one-size-fits-all, approach to supporting resilience. Taking time to find out what different employees are struggling with, even those who belong to the same identity group, and what kinds of support they would like to have is a good use of employers’ time and effort.

JP: What are some of the most effective strategies to promote workplace resilience?

DKJ: It is important to remember that resilience is both personal and complex. Since it is personal, what one person needs to support their resilience may be completely different from what another needs. I can share four tips that are generally effective for individuals to foster resilience:

article continues after advertisement
  1. Recovery and rest: I can’t stress this one enough. Resilience takes effort and energy and can itself be very exhausting. Take time to protect and recover your energy, whether that is through taking a nap, a walk, a drive, a fun class, a vacation, and/or a call with a loved one.
  2. Social support: Community is key to overcoming. Humans are social beings. We are stronger together, and we are more motivated to persist when we know we are not alone. Take time to nurture close relationships and engage in mutual support. Vulnerably sharing our challenges can itself offer us relief, and helping others builds our connections.
  3. Emotion regulation and joy: When you feel ready, decide what you want to do with your emotions. If anything. For example, you always have the option to sit with and first accept your emotions. Then, if an emotion like anger is coming up, remember that it may be informative about what we value. Emotion regulation offers us options to deal with the understandable, but sometimes uncomfortable emotions that can arise during and persist after hard times. Again, this does not mean becoming upset about feelings or preventing negative emotions, but we can adjust our thoughts and situations when we are ready to shift our emotions. Behavior options like “situation selection”—removing ourselves from harmful contexts—and psychological options like “thoughts modification”—altering the way we look at a situation so it is more helpful to our growth and learning—are both emotion regulation strategies we can use. Also, it is really important to consistently make time for doing things we enjoy. Creating and allowing moments of joy is one of the most adaptive things we can do in the marathon of overcoming.
  4. Short- and long-term goal focus: Sometimes, to keep on going, we need to “zoom out”—focus on and remember our “why.” And sometimes, maybe immediately after an adversity, if we are under time pressure, we need to “zoom in”—just focus on the next step to take to move towards our goal. In hard times, our brain tends to “zoom in,” and that is adaptive for a time. But making sure we do not get “lost in the weeds” and that we take time to remember the “big picture” is useful for intrinsic motivation and long-term resilience. This infuses purpose and meaning into day-to-day tasks.

These are all individual strategies that are meant to be employed when adversity can’t be removed. Structural strategies, like support from organizational leaders and tangible resources that employees need to pursue their goals, also need to be present for adaptive resilience.

JP: What is the role of leadership and psychological safety?

DKJ: Leaders are very important for organizational resilience. Leaders often shape the climate of a place and determine access to resources. As an example of their important role, in one study, we found that two significant predictors of team resilience are voice climate and leaders’ learning goal orientation. Voice climate is whether people feel they can speak up safely with ideas and will be listened to if they offer suggestions. This voice process requires that employees feel psychological safety. And leader learning goal orientation is about whether leaders focus on learning, and not just performing.

High voice climate and greater leader learning orientation were shown to together foster team resilience. And in another study, we found that even when leaders are saying “no” to an idea or suggestion, it matters that they respond in a manner that is considerate and sensitive. Otherwise, people will stop speaking up, and this can be costly and dangerous. Overall, research shows that leaders can shape psychological safety and are a key part of the employee resilience puzzle.

JP: How should employers measure employee resilience?

DKJ: This is a great and complex question. Measurement in psychological sciences is hard—this is why I say we are not a “soft” science! How you measure a thing needs to be guided by and aligned with how you define it.

So, we have published a chapter called “What is resilience” to theoretically ground our definition and offer more clarity, and we recently developed and are currently validating a new measure of employee resilience. We did this because we uncovered some limitations within existing definitions and measures and wanted to contribute knowledge to this conversation. What is most important is that decision-makers define resilience clearly and then choose a measure that aligns with that conceptualization. It is also useful to consider measuring individual experiences, such as goals and adversity, when measuring this concept.

item.title: The Benefits of Agency
item.description:
Career

The Benefits of Agency

Agency comes from how you think, feel, and act.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • I can act persistently and intelligently in pursuit of my goals.
  • Human progress comes from people setting goals and achieving them.
  • Look for your demands blocking you from this pursuit.

According to American psychologist Martin Seligman, in his book Agency: The Psychological History of Human Progress, progress over the centuries has resulted partly from people's belief that they have agency.

Agency is the idea, when based in reality, that one can make choices and take actions in ways that positively influence one's life.

Agency is based on how you think, feel, and act. There has been progress throughout the centuries because humans have set goals and then acted with persistence, intelligence, and rationality in their efforts to achieve these goals. It is essential to have a strong preference, desire, and determination in the pursuit of your objectives, without thinking in terms of musts and demands in your efforts.

Suppose you're out of work and seeking employment

Demands and other irrational thinking to avoid that tend to sabotage agency:

  • I must have a guarantee of success.
  • I must seek a job in the best way possible.
  • It must not be difficult to get a job.
  • I must find work right now.
  • I can't stand the hassles involved.
  • It must be easy to find a job.
  • I must get a job that is a perfect fit.

Here's an example of a cognitive-behavioral exercise, also called a Three-Minute Exercise, you can practice to change your thinking and develop a constructive sense of agency:

A. (Activating Event) I'm currently unemployed and seeking a job.

B. (Irrational Belief) It must be easy to find employment.

C. (Undesirable Emotional Consequences) Powerless and hopeless.

D. (Questioning or Debating the Irrational Belief) What is the evidence that supports my belief that it must be easy to find employment?

E. (Effective New Thinking or the Answer to the Question) There exists no proof or logic to support my conviction that it must be quick and easy to find employment. Although I strongly prefer it to be quick and easy to get a job, no evidence exists that it absolutely must be. Although I do not like this difficult situation, I can rationally stand what I do not like. I have survived financially challenging situations in the past and I will survive this one. At the very worst, I will have great disadvantages from being out of work, but never an end-of-the-world scenario.

F. (New Feeling and Behavior Resulting From E.) Frustrated, regretful, and disappointed yet determined to put more effort into finding employment. Consult a career counselor to assist me in my efforts.

G. (Give myself an action assignment.) Update my resume. Spend two hours daily contacting employers and businesses in my area or the U.S. which may be a good fit. Consider taking courses to update my knowledge and skills.

item.title: A Thought Is Not Always a Confession
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

A Thought Is Not Always a Confession

How I learned to question my thoughts instead of accepting them as facts.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • Loving a child and grieving life before motherhood can coexist without making someone a bad parent.
  • Recovery can involve tolerating uncertainty rather than waiting to feel completely sure of oneself.
  • Everyday acts of care are part of mothering, even when feelings of connection fluctuate.

During treatment for postpartum depression, a therapist asked me a question I later wrote in my journal: Can you live in the in-between for now?

At the time, my answer was no. I wanted certainty. I wanted someone to tell me my daughter would sleep. That I would sleep. That I loved her enough. That I was a good mother. That I would recover. That I would become myself again.

Instead, I had Lily—a real baby who changed every day. And I had a mind that sometimes changed by the hour.

One morning I could believe my daughter deserved another mother. Later that same day, we'd take a walk. She'd be bundled beneath a blanket, full and peaceful, and I'd write: I loved being her mother this afternoon.

Not forever. Not perfectly. That afternoon.

Recovery began when that became enough.

One afternoon, Lily started rolling from her back onto her stomach. She was still tiny. Once she realized she was face-down, she panicked. She screamed. I turned her over. She looked at me and smiled.

In my journal, I tried to describe that smile. It seemed to me that she knew exactly who I was. She had been frightened. She called and I came.

Then I wrote: That felt good. I felt like her mom.

One of the most important things I learned in treatment was remarkably simple: Sometimes thoughts are just thoughts. I practiced this almost like a mantra. When my mind said, I can't do this anymore: Just a thought.

When I imagined escaping: Just a thought.

When a difficult day made me wonder whether becoming a mother had destroyed my life: Just a thought.

That didn't mean ignoring dangerous symptoms. I needed serious help. Some thoughts required immediate attention. But I started to understand that having a thought didn't automatically make it truth. A desire wasn't an intention. And a thought didn't have to become who I was. Who I would be.

I think there was something else underneath my obsession with escaping. I missed myself. I missed writing. I missed my husband. I missed slow mornings. I missed eating without interruption. I missed the woman whose body and time seemed to belong to her. I thought becoming a good mother meant I had to get rid of that woman.

So whenever I missed her, I interpreted grief as rejection of Lily. But I know now that I can mourn a life that ended without wishing away the life that followed. I know now that it's possible to love our children and miss who we were before them. That we can feel grateful and trapped. That we can want closeness and solitude. And that we can have a terrible morning and a beautiful afternoon. It's also possible, and maybe even radical to say, that we can be mothers and still be people, ourselves even.

I used to believe recovery would arrive as certainty, like a flipped switch. I imagined waking up one morning and just knowing this: I am a good mother. Instead, recovery was only ordinary. I went back to work. I ate. I slept. I missed Lily while I was away from her.

My husband sent me photographs during the day: Lily eating prunes, doing tummy time, trying to stand. Suddenly she was approaching six months. Where had the time gone?

Then one afternoon I was driving home from work when a familiar thought appeared: I don't want to do this anymore. Mom. Momming. Being Mom.

Months earlier, that thought could have swallowed the entire day. I would have questioned it, followed it. I might have used it as proof that something was wrong with me. This time I simply breathed out: This is just a thought. Again. Just a thought. And I kept driving home, with or without it.

That moment seems small compared with hospitalization, medication, therapy, and everything else that happened during my postpartum illness. But looking back, I think it was enormous. The thought came. I didn't have to go with it.

For months I kept asking myself: Am I really her mother? I understand the question differently now. I thought motherhood was supposed to be a feeling—some permanent state of certainty and overwhelming love that would prove I was the right person to do this work.

But motherhood appeared as action. It meant turning Lily over. Giving her a bath. Brushing her hair. Going to therapy. Going back to work. Coming home. Choosing to stay. I had stopped waiting for permission to be her mother. I was doing it.

Living in the in-between meant love and disappointment could coexist. I could love my daughter and still struggle with being her mom. These feelings didn't get to define who I was as a mother.

The thoughts would come and they would go. But through treatment, I realized they didn't control whether I could keep going home.
